<b>Altura de la estrella</b><br>Es el án:
Star altitude
It is the angle between the horizon and the star at the moment of recording: 0° on the horizon and 90° right above you (the zenith).

What is it for? Near the horizon the light crosses more air and the measured seeing comes out worse. With the altitude, TurbuLENS also calculates the zenith seeing, which lets you compare different nights and stars: εzenith = ε · (cos z)3/5, with z = 90° − altitude.

How do I get it? In a planetarium program or app (for example Stellarium), with your observing site and the date and time of the recording: look up the star and copy its «altitude». It can be typed with decimals (for example 63.25°).

If you don't know it, leave the box unchecked: the rest of the analysis doesn't change.

Cuando tenemos <b>dos variables</b> para:
When we have two variables for each frame, a scatter plot puts one on the x axis and the other on the y axis. The correlation coefficient r goes from −1 to 1:
• r ≈ 1: when one goes up, so does the other;
• r ≈ −1: when one goes up, the other goes down;
• r ≈ 0: there is no linear relationship.

The atmosphere has a short «memory»: one frame resembles the next (high r) but not one half a second later. This shows that turbulence changes within milliseconds.
Cuando una medición depende de muchísimo:
When a measurement depends on a great many small random effects (like thousands of air bubbles), the data usually form a bell: the normal or Gaussian distribution.

The bell is defined only by the mean x̄ and the deviation σ, and follows the 68–95–99.7 rule:
• about 68 % of the data lie within 1 σ of the mean,
• about 95 % within 2 σ,
• almost all (99.7 %) within 3 σ.

Compare the percentages of your real data with those of the theory.

Imagina que miras una moneda en el fondo:
Imagine looking at a coin at the bottom of a swimming pool. If the water is still, you see it sharply. If someone stirs the water, the coin trembles and looks blurry.

The same happens with stars: their light crosses the Earth's air, which has warm and cold bubbles moving all the time. Those bubbles bend the light a tiny bit and the star seems to dance and twinkle.

The seeing is a number that says how much the star dances. It is measured in «arcseconds» (″), a very small unit of angle: 1″ is the size of a 1 cm coin seen from 2 km away.

The smaller the seeing, the sharper the sky and the better for observing.
La <b>media</b> (promedio) suma todos lo:
The mean (average) adds up all the data and divides by how many there are (formula below).

The median is the middle value when we sort them from smallest to largest: half of the data lies below and the other half above.

If the data are symmetric, mean and median almost coincide. If there are very odd data, the mean gets dragged along and the median barely moves: we say the median is robust.

Si tomamos solo unos pocos cuadros al az:
If we take just a few frames at random, their mean changes every time. If we repeat that thousands of times, the means also form a bell (this is the central limit theorem).

The width of that bell of means is the standard error of the mean (formula below).

That's why we record thousands of frames: with 4 times more frames the error is cut in half; with 100 times more, to a tenth.

Tapamos el telescopio con una cartulina:
We cover the telescope with a piece of cardboard that has two little holes. That way the starlight comes in through two different paths and we see two spots instead of one.

If the telescope shakes (because of the wind or because someone touches it), both spots move together. But air turbulence affects each path differently, so the spots move closer together and farther apart from each other.

That's why we don't measure where the star is, but the distance between the two spots. That distance changes a little in every frame of the video, and the statistics of those changes tell us the seeing.

Un <b>dato atípico</b> está muy lejos de:
An outlier is very far from the rest. It can be real or a measurement error.

A true story: in the original program this project started from, 68 frames of the Altair video showed only one spot. The program paired them wrongly and produced false distances close to 0 px. With only 68 bad data points out of 8,484, the standard deviation almost doubled and the seeing came out worse than it really was.

TurbuLENS detects those frames and also applies a robust clipping: it discards the data that lie more than 5 «robust σ» from the median (it uses the MAD, which is not dragged by the extremes).

Una <b>medición</b> es un número que obt:
A measurement is a number we get by observing something. Here we measure the distance between the two spots of the star's image, in pixels (px).

Each frame of the video gives one data point. With a 2-minute video at 60 frames per second we have more than 8,000 data points of the same variable.

The data we have are a sample. The population would be all the possible measurements of that night. With statistics we use the sample to learn about the population.
